lessons.title: Whole Wheat and Graham Flour Production
lessons.body: Whole wheat flour is made by grinding the entire wheat kernelâbran, germ, and endospermâso nothing is removed. To produce it, start with clean, dry wheat (moisture below 14%). Use a stone mill or a hammer mill. If using a stone mill, set the stones to a gap of about 0.5 mm for a fine grind. For a coarser graham flour, increase the gap to 1 mm. The bran and germ contain oils that can go rancid, so whole wheat flour has a shelf life of only 2â3 months in a cool, dry place. In Africa, where humidity is high, store in airtight containers with a desiccant or in a refrigerator. Graham flour is simply a coarser whole wheat flour, named after Sylvester Graham. It is not sifted, so it retains all the bran. To make 1 kg of whole wheat flour, you need about 1.1 kg of wheat berries, as some loss occurs during cleaning and milling. A small hammer mill (e.g., 5 HP) can produce 100â150 kg per hour. After milling, let the flour cool before packaging to prevent condensation. Use whole wheat flour within 3 months for best baking results. It absorbs more water than white flour, so when baking bread, add 2â3 tablespoons extra water per cup of flour. In many African markets, whole wheat flour is prized for its nutritional value and nutty flavor. You can also blend it with cassava flour to reduce cost and improve local availability.

lessons.title: High-Gluten and Low-Gluten Flours
lessons.body: Gluten is the protein that gives bread its structure and chew. High-gluten flour contains 12â14% protein, while low-gluten flour has 6â9%. To make high-gluten flour, you need hard wheat varieties like hard red spring or hard red winter. Mill them finely and sift out some bran to concentrate the protein. A typical high-gluten flour for bagels or pizza has 13% protein. In Africa, hard wheat is grown in Ethiopia, Kenya, and South Africa. If you cannot get hard wheat, you can add vital wheat gluten (a powder) to all-purpose flour: for every 1 kg of flour, add 50â100 g of vital wheat gluten to raise protein by 1â2%. Low-gluten flour is made from soft wheat varieties like soft red winter or soft white. These are milled and sifted to remove much of the protein-rich germ and bran. Cake flour is a good example, with 7â8% protein. To test protein content without a lab, mix 100 g of flour with 50 ml of water, knead into a dough, then wash it under running water to remove starch. The remaining sticky mass is gluten. Weigh it: if it weighs 12 g or more, it's high-gluten; if under 9 g, it's low-gluten. Store high-gluten flour in a dry place; it can last 6â8 months. Low-gluten flour lasts about 6 months. Use high-gluten for yeast breads, low-gluten for cakes, biscuits, and pastries. In many African bakeries, blending high and low gluten flours allows you to create custom breads for local tastes.

lessons.title: Organic and Stone-Ground Flours
lessons.body: Organic flour is milled from wheat grown without synthetic pesticides or fertilizers. To be certified organic, the wheat must be grown on land free from prohibited substances for at least 3 years. In Africa, organic wheat is grown in Egypt, Tunisia, and South Africa. Stone-ground flour is made by grinding wheat between two large stones, usually granite or quartz. The stones rotate slowly (about 100â200 rpm), which keeps the flour cool (below 40Â°C) and preserves nutrients and flavor. In contrast, steel roller mills generate heat that can damage vitamins. To set up a stone mill, you need a pair of matched stones, a motor (1â5 HP), and a feeding mechanism. A small stone mill can produce 20â50 kg per hour. The stones must be dressed (sharpened) every 200â300 hours of use. Stone-ground flour is typically whole grain, but you can sift it to make a lighter flour. It has a shorter shelf life (2â3 months) because the germ oil is exposed. Store in a cool, dark place or refrigerate. Organic stone-ground flour commands a premium price in urban African markets. For example, in Nairobi, a 1 kg bag sells for 2â3 times the price of conventional flour. To start, source organic wheat from certified farms, mill with a stone mill, and package in paper bags with a label stating 'organic' and 'stone-ground'. You can also offer custom milling services for local farmers. Keep records of your organic sourcing to maintain certification.

lessons.title: Ancient Grain Flours (Spelt, Einkorn, Emmer)
lessons.body: Ancient grains like spelt, einkorn, and emmer are older wheat varieties that have not been hybridized. Spelt (Triticum spelta) has a tough hull that must be removed before milling. It has 12â15% protein but weaker gluten, so it makes flatbreads and cookies well. Einkorn (Triticum monococcum) is the oldest wheat, with 14â18% protein but very weak gluten. Emmer (Triticum dicoccum), also called farro, has 12â14% protein and a nutty flavor. To mill these grains, use a stone mill or a burr mill. Set the gap to 0.4â0.6 mm for fine flour. Because the grains are smaller and harder than modern wheat, you may need to adjust the mill. For einkorn, mill at a slower speed to avoid overheating. Yields are lower: 1 kg of einkorn berries yields about 800 g of flour because of the hull. In Africa, these grains are not widely grown, but you can import them or source from local organic farmers. Spelt is the easiest to find. Use ancient grain flours in blends with modern wheat to improve structure. For example, replace 25% of wheat flour with spelt flour in a bread recipe. Store these flours in airtight containers in the refrigerator; they go rancid quickly due to high oil content. They are popular in health food markets and can be sold at a premium. Start with small batches and test baking to understand their behavior.

lessons.title: Gluten-Free Flours and Blends
lessons.body: Gluten-free flours are made from grains, seeds, and nuts that do not contain gluten. Common ones include rice flour, maize flour, millet flour, sorghum flour, teff flour, and cassava flour. To make rice flour, mill white or brown rice in a hammer mill or stone mill. Set the gap to 0.3 mm for fine flour. Brown rice flour is more nutritious but has a shorter shelf life (2â3 months) due to oils. Maize flour is made by milling dried maize kernels; in Africa, this is often done with a diesel-powered hammer mill. For a fine gluten-free flour, mill twice and sift through a 60-mesh sieve. Teff flour, from Ethiopia, is very fine and has a high calcium content. To make a gluten-free blend that works for bread, combine 60% rice flour, 20% potato starch, and 20% tapioca starch. Add 1 teaspoon of xanthan gum per cup of blend to mimic gluten. Without xanthan gum, use 1 tablespoon of ground flaxseed mixed with 3 tablespoons of water per cup. Gluten-free flours absorb more water, so add 10â20% more liquid. Store in airtight containers in a cool, dry place. In many African countries, gluten-free products are in demand for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance. You can mill local grains like millet, sorghum, and teff to create affordable gluten-free flours. Test your blends by baking small loaves; adjust gums and liquids until you get a good rise.

lessons.title: Custom Blending for Bakery Applications
lessons.body: Custom blending means mixing different flours to achieve specific baking qualities. Bakers blend for protein content, flavor, cost, and nutrition. For bread, you want 12â14% protein. If you have high-gluten flour (14%) and low-gluten flour (8%), mix them in a ratio to get 12%: use 2 parts high-gluten to 1 part low-gluten. For cakes, aim for 7â9% protein: mix 1 part high-gluten with 3 parts low-gluten. To blend, use a ribbon blender or a cement mixer (clean) for large batches. Mix for 10â15 minutes until uniform. Test the blend by making a small dough and checking elasticity. For whole wheat bread, blend 70% whole wheat flour with 30% white bread flour to improve rise. For a nutritious porridge blend, mix 50% maize flour, 30% sorghum flour, and 20% soy flour. In Africa, custom blending allows you to use local grains like cassava, millet, and teff to reduce reliance on imported wheat. For example, a bakery in Ghana might blend 60% wheat flour with 40% cassava flour for a cheaper bread. But cassava has no gluten, so add 2% vital wheat gluten per kilogram of blend. Always label your blends with ingredients and protein content. Store blended flours in moisture-proof bags. Keep records of your recipes so you can repeat successful blends. Start with small batches (10 kg) and scale up after testing.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between whole wheat flour and white flour?
options: A) Whole wheat includes bran and germ; white removes them
B) Whole wheat is made from soft wheat; white from hard wheat
C) Whole wheat has more gluten than white
D) Whole wheat is always stone-ground
quiz.explanation: Whole wheat flour retains all parts of the kernel, while white flour removes bran and germ.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for wheat before milling?
quiz.explanation: Wheat should be dry, with moisture below 14%, to prevent mold and ensure good milling.

quiz.q: How long can whole wheat flour be stored in a cool, dry place?
quiz.explanation: Whole wheat flour contains oils from the germ that go rancid after 2-3 months.

quiz.q: What is graham flour?
options: A) A type of white flour
B) A coarse whole wheat flour
quiz.explanation: Graham flour is a coarser grind of whole wheat flour that retains all bran.

quiz.q: How much wheat berries are needed to produce 1 kg of whole wheat flour?
quiz.explanation: About 1.1 kg of wheat berries yields 1 kg of flour due to loss during cleaning and milling.

quiz.q: What is the protein content of high-gluten flour?
quiz.explanation: High-gluten flour typically contains 12-14% protein, ideal for bread.

quiz.q: Which wheat variety is best for making low-gluten flour?
quiz.explanation: Soft wheat varieties like soft red winter have lower protein, suitable for low-gluten flour.

quiz.q: How can you increase the protein content of all-purpose flour?
quiz.explanation: Vital wheat gluten is a powder that boosts protein when added to flour.

quiz.q: What is a simple test to estimate gluten content?
options: B) Wash dough under water and weigh gluten
quiz.explanation: Kneading dough and washing away starch leaves gluten, which can be weighed.

quiz.q: What is the typical protein content of cake flour?
quiz.explanation: Cake flour has about 7-8% protein, which gives a tender crumb.

quiz.q: What is required for wheat to be certified organic?
options: A) Grown without pesticides for 3 years
C) Milled in a steel mill
quiz.explanation: Organic certification requires land free from prohibited substances for at least 3 years.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of stone-ground flour?
options: C) Preserves nutrients due to cool milling
quiz.explanation: Stone milling generates less heat, preserving vitamins and flavor.

quiz.q: How often should stone mill stones be dressed?
quiz.explanation: Stones need sharpening (dressing) after about 200-300 hours of use.

quiz.q: What is the shelf life of stone-ground whole wheat flour?
quiz.explanation: Stone-ground whole wheat flour has exposed germ oils and lasts 2-3 months.

quiz.q: Which ancient grain has the highest protein content?
quiz.explanation: Einkorn has 14-18% protein, higher than spelt and emmer.

quiz.q: What is a challenge when milling einkorn?
options: B) It has a tough hull
quiz.explanation: Einkorn has a tough hull that must be removed before milling.

quiz.q: What is the typical yield of flour from einkorn berries?
quiz.explanation: About 800 g of flour is obtained from 1 kg of einkorn berries due to hull loss.

quiz.q: How should ancient grain flours be stored?
quiz.explanation: Ancient grain flours have high oil content and should be refrigerated to prevent rancidity.

quiz.q: Which of these is a gluten-free flour?
quiz.explanation: Teff is naturally gluten-free, while spelt, einkorn, and emmer contain gluten.

quiz.q: What is xanthan gum used for in gluten-free baking?
quiz.explanation: Xanthan gum helps bind gluten-free doughs and improve texture.

quiz.q: How much xanthan gum is typically added per cup of gluten-free flour blend?
quiz.explanation: About 1 teaspoon of xanthan gum per cup of flour blend is standard.

quiz.q: Which grain is commonly milled into gluten-free flour in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Millet is a gluten-free grain widely grown and milled in Africa.

quiz.q: What is a good substitute for xanthan gum in gluten-free baking?
options: B) Ground flaxseed mixed with water
quiz.explanation: Ground flaxseed mixed with water forms a gel that can replace xanthan gum.

quiz.q: Why do gluten-free flours often require more liquid?
quiz.explanation: Gluten-free flours absorb more water than wheat flour, so recipes need extra liquid.

quiz.q: What is the target protein content for bread flour?
quiz.explanation: Bread flour typically has 12-14% protein for good structure.

quiz.q: If you mix 2 parts high-gluten flour (14% protein) with 1 part low-gluten flour (8% protein), what is the approximate protein content of the blend?
quiz.explanation: The weighted average is (2*14 + 1*8)/3 = 12%.

quiz.q: What equipment can be used for blending flours in large batches?
quiz.explanation: A ribbon blender is designed for uniform mixing of dry powders.

quiz.q: Why is cassava flour often blended with wheat flour in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Cassava flour is cheaper and locally available, reducing reliance on imported wheat.

quiz.q: What must be added to a cassava-wheat blend to improve bread quality?
quiz.explanation: Cassava has no gluten, so vital wheat gluten is added to provide structure.

quiz.q: What should be included on a label for a custom flour blend?
quiz.explanation: Labels should list ingredients and protein content for consumer information.
